title: Rivet: angels, if present, would be received; being unseen and not everywhere, they are not greeted
source_text: XXXVIII. Andreas Rivetus autem sic pluribus philosophatur de honore qui debetur creaturis rationalibus, sive Angeli, sive homines sint. Si adsint, inquit, Angeli, id nobis incognitum est quando, & ubi, nisi aliquando visibili specie, ut olim factum est, nobis appareant. Alioquin aliquos nobis adesse saepius, & nos juvare novimus: sed quia nobis non est cum eis sermonis commercium, nec ubique sunt, nec cordium nostrorum recessus scrutantur: ideo non solemus cum iis verba commutare, neque signis externis eos salutare. Quod cum praesentibus hominibus facimus, & cum Angelis olim fecerunt Patriarchae, qui domi suae exceperunt, quos homines putarunt. Extra hanc occasionem de Angelis loquimur (Angelus suos intelligo) cum honore & reverentia, eorum naturam, officia, obediendi Deo promptitudinem magnifacimus, & hanc nobis imitandam proponimus.
pass_a_gloss: Andrew Rivet philosophizes at more length about the honor owed to rational creatures, whether they are angels or men. If angels are present, he says, it is unknown to us when and where, unless they sometimes appear to us in a visible form, as was once done. Otherwise we know that some are often present to us and help us: but because we have no commerce of speech with them, nor are they everywhere, nor do they search the recesses of our hearts, therefore we do not usually exchange words with them, nor greet them with outward signs. Which we do with men who are present, and which the patriarchs once did with angels, whom they received in their house, taking them for men. Apart from this occasion we speak of angels (I mean his own angels) with honor and reverence, we magnify their nature, their offices, their readiness to obey God, and we set this before ourselves to be imitated.
pass_b_english: Rivet treats honor of rational creatures, angels and humans, together.
If angels are present we do not know when or where, unless they appear visibly as they once did.
Some are often near and helpful, but there is no conversation with them, they are not everywhere, and they do not search the heart, so we neither speak to them nor greet them with outward signs.
The patriarchs did greet angels whom they received as men; apart from that, angels are spoken of with honor, and their obedience is magnified for imitation.

choices.why: External greeting belongs only to an appearance, as with the patriarchs.
rejected: a permanent presence that warrants invocation
